| | Week 1: developed market | Week 2: emerging market |
|:-------|:----------------|:----------------|
| Data | 2021-24, 163,150 claims; 626,639 rows to price | 2023-24, 9,258 claims; 209,063 rows to price |
| Submitted file | geometric mean of six experts, recalibrated per line | v13: ensemble ranking, segment levels read from the leaderboard |
| Public / private D² | 0.12851 / **0.13830** | **0.17172** / pending (v12, public 0.17095, also selected) |

Both weeks are scored on the Tweedie deviance D² with power 1.5, pooled over the three lines. My
first Week 2 file, a plain LightGBM, scored 0.12519. The work rests on three choices. I spent time
on the target before building any model. In the new market I started from what the developed market
already knew and let the local data correct it. And I kept a segment's level separate from the
ranking inside it, because the 2025 book is too different from the training years for a back-test
to say what the levels should be.

# Data and target

Both weeks go through the same scripts (read, clean, build features), and each one has an executed
notebook next to it as evidence. Every fix is logged with the rows it changed. I dropped no rows and
imputed nothing. The audit found customer ids that had lost their leading zeros (123,664 rows),
exposure recorded in days or on a 360-day basis (13,880 and 595 rows in the two weeks), sums insured
entered in units instead of thousands (3,527 and 349), a case reserve typed with an extra digit
(11.9m instead of 1.19m), and impossible years licensed, which I restored from the same policy's
other years (3,717 rows). The last one found, after Week 1 had been submitted, was 604 claims stored
twice under a second id. They had inflated 2022 claim counts by 1.4%.

**Target.** The ultimate cost of the claims with a loss date inside the row's period, net of excess
and recoveries, with repudiated claims left out. Claims are valued at 31 December 2024, so 2024 is
not fully reported: only about half of its bodily-injury cost is in. Every model's offset is
log(exposure × share of claims reported), with the share taken from a reporting pattern per peril.
Open claims are developed with the recovery ratio seen on closed ones, costs are trended to 2025 per
peril, and costs above the 99.5% quantile are capped and added back as a load per line (1.02 to 1.06).

**Feature selection.** A column stays only if it beats 20 random "probe" columns out of time, both
on its own and inside a small LightGBM. The pass mark lets at most 1 in 20 noise columns through.
Week 1 keeps 53, 44 and 49 features (motor, buildings, contents). Week 2 keeps only 28, 14 and 9,
because two years of a small book cannot prove the weaker effects.

# Week 1: six experts and a geometric mean

For each line I trained six experts, each three times: on 2021-22 to price 2023, on 2021-23 to
price 2024, and on all four years to price 2025. All of them are LightGBM with an exact log offset,
except the GLM.

| Expert | What it models |
|:-------|:----------------------------|
| `total` | Tweedie GBM on capped total cost, times the line's large-loss load |
| `glm` | Tweedie GLM on banded numeric factors and grouped categories |
| `peril` | one Tweedie GBM per peril, with its own reporting share and load, summed |
| `fs_gamma`, `fs_lognorm` | Poisson frequency × claim size (Gamma; or lognormal with a risk-specific variance) |
| `fs_peril` | frequency × claim size for each peril, summed |

The predictions are combined row by row with an equal-weight geometric mean, and each line is then
recalibrated with a two-parameter Tweedie GLM,
$\log E = \log(\text{exposure}\cdot L) + b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{geo}/L)$, where $L$ is the line's mean
rate. The GLM is fitted on the two back-test years; $b_1$ comes out at 1.04 for motor, 1.10 for
buildings and 1.09 for contents.

| Back-test D², all lines (calibration fitted on the other year) | 2023 | 2024 |
|:----------------------------|------:|------:|
| one LightGBM on total cost | 0.1364 | 0.1338 |
| best single expert (`fs_peril`) | 0.1379 | 0.1365 |
| geometric mean of the six, recalibrated | **0.1386** | **0.1375** |

The frequency × claim-size experts beat a single cost model in every line and year, and the six
together beat each one of them. A seventh expert, a mixture of experts for claim size, gave the same
private score, so I kept the simpler file. The table comes from the rebuilt pipeline. The file I
submitted came from the 22 October code, which reported 0.1380 and 0.1367 and was written before the
duplicate-claim and years-licensed fixes. Its 2025 predictions have a log correlation of 0.996 to
0.998 with the rebuild.

# Week 2: adapting to the emerging market

Week 2 differed from Week 1 in most of the ways that matter to a pricing model:

| | Week 1 | Week 2 |
|:--------|:----------|:------------------|
| History | 4 years, 163k claims | 2 years, 9k claims (about 1,000 per home line) |
| New business in the year priced | close to the training mix | 77% of 2025, against 12-15% of training rows |
| Gender | not a rating factor | a permitted rating factor |
| Weather of the year | inside the training range | 2025 far outside it (rainfall anomaly −128 mm against ±3 mm) |
| Buildings experience | stable | a 2023 fire-cost spike; 2024 came in at 0.59 of 2023's prediction |

**Transfer from the developed market.** I fit a LightGBM on every Week 1 row using only the factors
that mean the same thing in both markets (30 for motor, 24 for buildings, 26 for contents), always
with renewal count, and put its log rate into the offset of the Week 2 models. The local trees then
only have to learn how this market differs, and 20 to 110 trees are enough. Each Week 1 expert is
rebuilt the same way, on a prior for its own component (frequency, claim size, each peril). A peril
with fewer than 50 claims (300 for claim sizes) uses its prior alone, re-levelled. I dropped the
weather of the year.

**Choices made by cross-validation.** Two years give only one forward test, so the tuning used five
folds of customers over 2023-24. It picked one-split trees for motor and contents and a strong GLM
ridge; a weak ridge overfits buildings to a D² below zero. It also picked a member set per line
instead of all six experts (motor `total` + `fs_peril` + `glm`, buildings `fs_lognorm` + `peril`,
contents `total` + `glm`), because two years hold too few claims to learn claim sizes. The
recalibration slope stays at 1, since a slope fitted on one year did not carry to the other.
New-business and gender factors are measured on out-of-fold predictions and shrunk towards no effect.

| Forward test: fit on 2023, score 2024, all lines | D² |
|:----------------------------|------:|
| LightGBM on Week 2 data only | 0.1026 |
| developed-market prior alone | 0.1259 |
| LightGBM on top of the prior | 0.1277 |
| ensemble on priors | **0.1300** |

# What the leaderboard taught me

The ensemble (v4) scored 0.16198 in public. My earlier single transfer LightGBM had scored 0.16529,
even though the ensemble ranked the 2024 risks better. The gap came from the levels. The 2024
back-test is 13% new business and 2025 is 77%, so the back-test can judge the ranking inside a
segment but not the level of new business, buildings or gender.

So I treated ranking and level as two separate problems. For the ranking, v5 keeps the earlier
file's total in each of ten segments (line × new business × gender) and replaces the ranking inside
them with a 50/50 geometric blend of that file and my ensemble. On 2024 rows weighted to the 2025
mix, the blend ranks better (within-segment D² 0.1067 against 0.1016). v5 changed a quarter of the
rows by more than 10% and still scored exactly 0.16529. That surprised me, and it settled the
question: the public score hardly reacts to the ranking inside segments.

**Levels.** For Tweedie p = 1.5, multiplying a segment's predictions by $c$ changes the deviance by
exactly
$$\Delta D = 4\left[(c^{-1/2}-1)A + (c^{1/2}-1)B\right], \qquad A=\textstyle\sum y\,\mu^{-1/2},\quad B=\sum \mu^{1/2},$$
so the best level is $c^* = A/B$, and any scored file that differs from another only by segment
factors is a measurement of it. I fit one model, linear in the ten best levels, to 13 public scores.
It matches all of them within 0.0001, and when five were left out of the fit it predicted them up to
one constant offset. It says motor needs a much wider gender split than any model of 2023-24 gave:
new-business men about ×1.37 on v5, women about ×0.97 (@fig-levels).

**Luck.** The public score covers only a sample of the 2025 rows, so a segment's best level on that
sample is off by $\text{sd} = \sqrt{\phi / (\text{share}\cdot\sum\mu^{1/2})}$. At a 30% public share
that is 8% for motor new-business men, 13% for buildings new business and 24% for buildings
renewals. The model fits this luck as a separate term and gives two answers: the best levels for the
public rows (v13), and the best levels for the rows not yet scored (v12), which pulls the noisy
segments back towards v5.

v12 scored 0.17095 (expected 0.1708) and v13 0.17172 (expected 0.1714). Against v5, the model
expects v12 to gain 0.0042 on unseen rows and v13 0.0037, with an sd of about 0.0015. I selected both
on Kaggle. v12 is my best estimate for the final ranking; v13 only wins if the true levels are as
extreme as the public rows suggest. The Week 2 file in this submission is v13, my best score. I also
tried two last ranking changes: no this-year weather in the buildings and contents model, and a motor
spread of ×1.05. That file, v14, scored 0.17032, which is 0.0006 below v12 against a public-luck sd of
0.0008. The leaderboard cannot tell whether that is a real loss, so I did not select it.

**What the new market changed.** I stopped learning everything from local data: the developed market
supplies the relativities, and the emerging data corrects them. Simpler local models did better
(one-split trees, a strong ridge, fewer experts, no fitted slope). The back-test was no longer
enough, because 2025 is mostly new business, so I judged ranking and level on different evidence.
And I treated the public leaderboard as a noisy measurement to model rather than a score to push up.

# Major decisions

| Decision | Rejected | Evidence |
|:-------------------|:-----------|:--------------|
| Fix data errors with evidence; drop and impute nothing | dropping or imputing rows | cleaning log per round |
| Geometric mean of experts, recalibrated per line (Week 1) | one LightGBM | +0.0022 (2023) and +0.0037 (2024) back-test D² |
| Developed-market prior in the offset (Week 2) | Week 2-only models | +0.025 forward D² |
| Members per line by cross-validation; slope fixed at 1 | all six experts; fitted slope | contents: all six 0.1071 against `total` alone 0.1087 |
| Segment levels kept apart from ranking | trusting the back-test's levels | v4 0.16198 against v5 0.16529 |
| Aim at unseen rows rather than the public sample | chasing the public score | public luck sd 8% to 24% per segment |

# Use of AI

I worked alone, with an AI coding agent (Claude Code in VS Code) at every step. The agent wrote and
ran most of the code and drafted this write-up. I set the questions and decided what got built.

Most of the work was a long run of prompts that proposed ideas and tested them: the developed-market
prior, the expert ensembles, the segment-level probes, the public-luck model. Each idea became a
script and had to hold up out of time before it counted.

The prompts carried context that pointed the agent somewhere specific: the case study, the question
to answer, and what had already failed and why, which I kept in `KNOWLEDGE.md`. That kept it from
starting over or retrying dead ends.

I used different skills for different jobs. Two project skills in the repository
(`.claude/skills/data-scientist` and `ml-engineer`) set how the agent writes code and runs an
analysis: frame the problem first, test out of time, distrust its own gains, and keep the code
reproducible and under version control.

I did not accept a result from the same run that produced it. Each idea was questioned separately,
so the agent had to check its own work, and this caught real problems. Factor searches looked strong
when the same two years both chose and scored the factors; a permutation test then showed that real
factors pass no more often than shuffled ones, and only gender survived. A later review found a sign
error in the Week 1 contents frequency trend. It is documented, left in the code that reproduces the
submitted file, and fixed in the rebuild.

Nothing went into the pipeline or a submission until I had reviewed the plan and its evidence. I
chose the target definition, what counted as evidence, which files to submit and select, and when to
stop probing the leaderboard.

# Assumptions

* 2025 claims follow 2023-24 after trend (motor severity 0 to 7.9% a year depending on peril,
  buildings severity 6%, contents frequency 1.4% and severity 3.4%). Reporting patterns are stable,
  and open claims develop the way closed ones did.
* For factors defined the same way in both markets, the developed market's relativities are a
  reasonable starting point. The emerging market differs in level and in a few effects that the local
  models can learn.
* The public leaderboard rows are a random sample of 2025, about 30%. The order of v12 and v13 holds
  for any share from 20% to 50%.
* Gender is a permitted rating factor in the emerging market, as the case study states.

# Limitations

* Buildings is the part I trust least. There are only two years of emerging-market data, a few large
  claims decide the buildings public score, and its levels carry 8% to 10% uncertainty.
* The Week 2 levels rest partly on the public leaderboard. The competition allows that, but in real
  pricing it would mean calibrating on a sample of the book's own outcomes, and the bands in
  @fig-levels are wide.
* Back-tests cannot judge new-business levels, and ranking changes such as v14 are smaller than the
  noise in the public score.
* The submitted Week 1 file still has the contents trend sign error. The per-line recalibration
  absorbs most of it (the intercept is about +10%), but the contents relativities may be slightly off.

# Guardrails

* Columns driven by the outcome are excluded: `renewal_decision`, and `customer_service_contacts`,
  which is zero on 0.2% of rows with a claim against 67% of rows without one. Claims history is built
  as it was known on 1 January of each year, so no feature looks ahead.
* The written premium is excluded, because a model using it would copy the old tariff. So are
  marketing and service fields and personal data such as surname. Gender is used only where it is
  permitted, and its factor moves price between men and women without changing a line's total.
* Every file is tested out of time before it is submitted, then registered as a new numbered version
  with its evidence, description and checksum. Versions are never overwritten.
* A file is saved only if it has one row per sample row id, in the sample's order, with every
  prediction finite and positive. The Week 1 code adds block and escalate rules: a back-test D² at
  or below zero blocks the file; an A/E outside 1 ± 5%, feature drift with a PSI of 0.25 or more, or
  a pure-premium shift of more than 15% against history goes to actuarial sign-off.
* Probe columns in feature selection, permutation tests on factor searches and the public-luck model
  are all there to stop me fitting noise, including apparent gains that an AI agent reports with
  confidence.
* Every step is a script under git. The data steps give the same bytes on every run, and the Week 1
  file rebuilds from cached expert predictions in a minute (largest relative difference 2e-15).
